headline: Hao Yan and Nicholas Zhao cut Falcon-512's signature from 666 to 419 bytes by analysing the distribution of accepted signatures directly instead of bounding the NTRU lattice's smoothing parameter, leaving the security target unchanged.

items.title: Where the photon lands sets the jitter of a wide strip detector
items.dek: A JPL, NIST and Geneva group scanned a focused laser across a 20-micrometre-wide tungsten-silicide superconducting strip — a single-photon detector wide enough to swallow a whole fibre spot — and found its timing spread is set by where across the strip the photon lands.
items.why_it_matters: That makes jitter a current-distribution problem rather than a film problem: the same device goes from 48.8 to 28.4 picoseconds of raw spread once a parallel superconducting rail pulls bias current away from the strip's edges, with nothing changed about the material or the geometry. It also undercuts a plan the field had for these detectors — reading how many photons arrived from the shape of the pulse — because the pulse now encodes where the photon landed as well as how many there were, and a wide strip has a lot of places to land.
items.background_md: A superconducting single-photon detector is a strip of superconductor carrying a bias current just below the value that would destroy superconductivity. One absorbed photon breaks enough Cooper pairs to drive a short section resistive, and the voltage step that follows is the click. How precisely that click marks the arrival time depends on how fast the step rises against the amplifier's noise floor — the slew rate. Nanowires about a hundred nanometres across give the fastest edges but must be meandered back and forth to cover a fibre mode; strips micrometres wide cover it in one pass, and let bias current crowd along their edges.
items.deeper_md:
The device is a 20 µm × 300 µm WSi strip, `T_c` 3.1 K, 843 Ω sheet resistance, biased at 645 µA at 0.9 K — 0.3 `T_c`. Slew-rate-corrected jitter is 13.2 ps at 532 nm and 20.5 ps at 1550 nm, with internal detection efficiency saturated out to 1550 nm. Scanning a free-space spot across the strip shows edge absorptions rising faster than centre ones, so the raw histogram is bimodal at 48.8 ps; 14.4 mA through a parallel rail moves supercurrent inward, closes the mismatch to 28.4 ps, and suppresses thermally activated dark counts enough to run at 1.625 K, or 0.54 `T_c`.

Two limits the authors set themselves. The time-dependent Ginzburg–Landau simulations that reproduce the position dependence were run at 4 µm width, not 20 µm, so the model is qualitative for this device; and they call the spatial slew variance a fundamental challenge for photon-number-resolving schemes built on wide strips. For scale, a meandered NbN nanowire reached 2.7 ps at 400 nm, and a 2023 20 µm strip with a high-critical-current bank reported 29.8 ps jitter and about 78% system detection efficiency at 1550 nm.

glossary.definition: How fast the detector's output voltage rises, in volts per second. Arrival-time spread is roughly the amplifier's noise divided by this, so a slower edge buys a wider histogram.
The spread, in picoseconds, of recorded arrival times for photons that genuinely arrived at the same instant; quoted as the full width at half maximum of that distribution.
The chance that a photon already absorbed in the film produces a click. When it saturates with bias current, every absorbed photon is counted and the remaining loss is purely optical.

Operating temperature divided by the film's superconducting transition temperature; 0.3 is deeply superconducting, 0.54 is close enough to the transition that thermal fluctuations start producing false counts.

items.fab_angle: A 20 µm line is printable with the tools a teaching cleanroom already has, where a 100 nm nanowire needs electron-beam lithography — that is the practical argument for wide-strip detectors. What this result moves into the critical path instead is film and edge quality: jitter now depends on how bias current distributes across the strip, so sputtered-film thickness uniformity and etched sidewall straightness become part of the timing specification.

items.title: Nitrogen doping in SiC jumps at C/Si = 1 because the step edge changes hands
items.dek: Wataru Ota and five co-authors calculated why nitrogen — the standard n-type dopant in silicon-carbide power devices — incorporates abruptly faster on the carbon face of 4H-SiC once the carbon-to-silicon ratio in the growth gas passes 1.0: the atomic step edge changes what terminates it.
items.why_it_matters: SiC epitaxy sets its doping with the carbon-to-silicon ratio rather than with the nitrogen flow, and production recipes sit within a few hundredths of 1.0 — which is exactly where this calculation puts a step in the curve instead of a slope. A knob with a discontinuity inside its working range does not tolerate the same drift as one without. The discontinuity also exists on only one of the crystal's two polar faces, so a doping calibration measured on the silicon face cannot be carried across to the carbon face, and the two need different control strategies for the same dopant.
items.background_md: Silicon-carbide power devices are built on an epitaxial layer grown on a wafer sliced a few degrees off the basal plane, so growth advances by atoms attaching at exposed atomic steps rather than nucleating on flat terraces. Nitrogen dopes SiC n-type by substituting for carbon, which means it competes for sites with carbon arriving from the gas: raise the carbon-to-silicon ratio and you suppress nitrogen. That trade is called site competition, and it is how doping is actually set in a reactor. The crystal has two inequivalent polar faces, silicon and carbon, and they do not respond alike.
items.deeper_md:
The behaviour being explained is a discontinuous rise in nitrogen incorporation on vicinal 4H-SiC(000-1) — the carbon face — as C/Si moves from 1.0 to 1.5, with no counterpart on the silicon face. Ota and co-authors compute step-edge termination populations from first principles and find they flip sharply at C/Si = 1.0: below it the edge is silicon-terminated, above it a carbon–hydrogen-terminated edge dominates, and nitrogen substitution at that edge costs less energy. The doping jump is therefore a surface-chemistry transition, not a change in gas-phase supply.

Two things to hold against it. This is ab-initio energetics plus a statistical model of edge population, not a growth experiment — it explains published data rather than predicting new data, and it covers one face and one offcut. And the window production actually uses is narrow and sits just below the claimed discontinuity: a 2026 optimisation of n-doped 4H-SiC homoepitaxy at 1610 °C swept only C/Si of 0.90, 0.95 and 1.00, settling on 0.95 for 3.35% doping uniformity at roughly 6 × 10¹⁵ cm⁻³. Nobody has contested the calculation yet; it is a week old.

glossary.definition: Setting the dopant level by changing the carrier-gas ratio instead of the dopant flow: nitrogen occupies carbon sites, so more carbon in the feed leaves fewer sites for nitrogen to take.

A wafer sliced a few degrees away from a low-index crystal plane, so its surface is a staircase of terraces and atomic steps; growth then proceeds by step flow, which copies the substrate's stacking sequence.
The carbon-terminated polar face of the 4H polytype of silicon carbide. The opposite face, (0001), is silicon-terminated, and the two behave differently during growth and doping.
The ratio of carbon to silicon atoms delivered by the precursor gases, and the main lever a SiC epitaxy engineer has over both doping level and surface morphology.

items.fab_angle: The useful transferable point for anyone running a tube furnace or a CVD reactor: incorporation can be set by what terminates the growing surface rather than by what is in the gas. When a doping level shifts without a flow change, the first suspects are surface preparation, offcut and temperature at the wafer, not the mass-flow controllers.

items.title: Stack height, not power, is what caps a DRAM-on-GPU stack
items.dek: imec's ESSERC 2026 paper models DRAM stacked directly on top of a reticle-sized GPU instead of beside it, and finds peak temperature falls from 121.7 to 103.4 degrees Celsius when cooling cavities are interleaved between the memory tiers rather than sitting above them.
items.why_it_matters: The number that governs a volumetric memory stack turns out to be its height rather than its power: peak temperature tracks how far heat has to travel before it reaches a cooling cavity, so buying capacity by making the stack taller costs temperature, while buying the same capacity by thinning dies and interleaving more cavities does not. That reorders the design problem. You choose a cavity material and a stack height first, and the bandwidth and capacity you are allowed to ask for follow from that choice rather than setting it.
items.background_md: An AI accelerator's memory sits beside the logic die on a silicon interposer, joined by a few thousand wires running a couple of centimetres. Putting the memory on top instead shortens those wires to microns and multiplies how many of them you can run, and that is where the bandwidth would come from. The obstacle is thermal: DRAM has the tightest temperature limit in the package, because charge retention falls off exponentially with temperature, and stacking it over the logic places it downstream of the hottest thing in the system, with the heat having to leave through the memory.
items.deeper_md:
Under a reticle-scale non-uniform GPU power map the optimised HBM-on-GPU baseline peaks at 121.7 °C. A one-DRAM-one-cooling-cavity organisation 3 mm tall with silicon cavities drops that to 103.4 °C while supplying 202 GB at 58.8 TB/s; copper cavities at 5 mm give 100.2 °C and diamond 86.9 °C. Density costs temperature — two thinner DRAM tiers per cavity buy 674 GB and 117.6 TB/s but run at 118.7 °C — and adding a memory-controller and network-on-chip tier costs about 4 °C. Mold between dies costs 1–2 °C with silicon cavities but 5–6 °C with diamond: the better the cavity, the more the ordinary packaging material matters.

The stated conclusion is that stack height dominates peak temperature while cavity conductivity shifts the feasible region, and that bandwidth gains flatten once execution becomes compute-bound. The comparison point is the same group's IEDM 2025 study, where unmitigated 3D HBM-on-GPU ran at 141.7 °C and reached 70.8 °C only after double-sided cooling plus halving the core clock, at a 28% slowdown in training steps. Caveats: this is package-level simulation, the copper and diamond cavities are assumed rather than demonstrated, and no such stack has been built.

glossary.definition: A void built into the die stack and fed with coolant, so heat leaves each memory tier sideways instead of travelling up through every die above it to a lid.
A model of how power density varies across a full-field die, rather than a single average watts-per-square-millimetre figure. Hotspots, not the mean, set peak temperature.
Terabytes per second — the rate at which memory can hand data to the compute die. In a 3D stack it grows with the number of vertical connections rather than with clock frequency.
The set of stack geometries and cooling choices that keep every die under its own temperature limit; it is a boundary in a design space, not a single wattage figure.

items.fab_angle: The mold-compound numbers are the practical detail for a packaging engineer: mold between dies costs 1–2 °C with a silicon cavity but 5–6 °C with a diamond one. The better the heat-removal path you pay for, the more the ordinary materials wrapped around it become the limit, which is the usual shape of thermal engineering.

items.title: A TPU clocked per-multiply, not per-worst-case, runs 2.15× faster
items.dek: Three engineers at Utah State University ran a tensor processing unit near its threshold voltage, where gate delay becomes strongly dependent on both process variation and the operand values, and recovered the wasted timing margin by predicting each multiply-accumulate's delay and stalling only the slow ones.
items.why_it_matters: A synchronous chip's clock period is set by its slowest path under the worst combination of process variation and input data, so every operation that settles early hands its remaining slack to nobody. Near threshold that donated slack is most of the chip's available speed, because the spread of gate delay grows faster than its mean as the supply falls. Moving the margin decision from the global clock down to the individual operation converts that slack into frequency — 2.15× here — for 13% more area and a 1% average accuracy loss, a trade a matrix multiply can make and a pointer cannot.
items.background_md: Near-threshold computing runs logic at a supply voltage close to the transistor's threshold rather than well above it; for a 45 nm CMOS process that region is roughly 0.3 to 0.7 V. Energy per operation falls steeply, because switching energy scales with the square of the supply. Gate delay rises steeply too, and worse, the spread of the delay rises faster than its average: at low supply a small difference in threshold voltage between two nominally identical transistors becomes a large difference in speed. A synchronous design absorbs that spread by lengthening the clock until the slowest possible path fits.
items.deeper_md:
The framework, DSAC, keeps one fixed global reference clock and varies how many cycles an operation gets rather than retuning frequency. Three lightweight predictors — Hamming distance between successive operands, most-significant-bit position, and a hybrid — estimate how delay-sensitive each multiply-accumulate is and sort them into three timing tiers, enforced locally with dummy-hold cycles. A closed-loop controller watches actual timing violations and moves the tier thresholds at runtime, so the predictor does not have to be right in advance. On quantised deep-network benchmarks the most-significant-bit predictor holds average accuracy loss to 1% even at the most aggressive settings, for up to 1.55× better energy efficiency at 2.15× the baseline TPU's frequency and as little as 13% area overhead.

What to discount: these are simulated results on a benchmark set, the 1% is an average and not a bound, and the whole approach assumes the workload tolerates occasional wrong arithmetic. The manuscript is accepted at ACM TODAES, so it has been reviewed — which is more than most results in this brief. Nobody disputes that near-threshold timing is statistically hard; modelling failure rates at 0.5 V is its own active research problem.

glossary.definition: Operating logic at a supply voltage close to the transistor threshold. Switching energy falls with the square of the supply, while both gate delay and its variability rise.
The gap between when a signal actually settles and when the clock edge samples it. Positive slack is unused margin; negative slack is a latched wrong answer.
The multiply-and-add that a matrix multiplier repeats; in a systolic array hundreds of them advance in lockstep on one clock, so the slowest one sets the period for all.
An inserted idle cycle that gives one slow operation a second clock period to settle, so the global clock does not have to be slowed down for every other operation.

items.title: Drop the smoothing estimate and Falcon's signature loses a third of its bytes
items.dek: Hao Yan and Nicholas Zhao posted a variant of Falcon — the lattice signature scheme NIST picked for FIPS 206 — that analyses the distribution of accepted signatures directly instead of bounding the NTRU lattice's smoothing parameter, and gets 419-byte signatures where Falcon-512 needs 666.
items.why_it_matters: Signature size is the reason a second lattice signature scheme was standardised at all: every byte is repeated in every certificate in a chain and in every handshake that presents one, so the on-the-wire cost of a post-quantum transition is mostly this number. A third fewer bytes at the same security target says the old parameters were paying for the looseness of a proof rather than for real margin — the saving comes from characterising what the sampler actually emits instead of bounding what it might emit. That is a different kind of improvement from a faster implementation, and a harder one to check.
items.background_md: Lattice signature schemes in the GPV family sign by sampling a short vector from a discrete Gaussian over a lattice whose secret basis is the signing key. The width of that Gaussian is the security-critical knob: too narrow and the samples betray which basis produced them, too wide and the signature takes more bits to write down. The width at which the distribution, folded onto the lattice, becomes flat enough to leak nothing is called the smoothing parameter. Nobody can compute it exactly, so schemes prove an upper bound on it and set the sampling width from that bound.
items.deeper_md:
The reported sizes are 419 bytes at ring degree 512 and 921 bytes at degree 1024, against Falcon's own 666 and 1280 — 37.09% and 28.05% smaller — and 11.60% and 5.92% smaller than the best previously published tightening, which the paper calls FALCON_WS. The change is in the analysis rather than the construction: instead of estimating the NTRU lattice's smoothing parameter and choosing a Gaussian width that clears it, the authors characterise the distribution of preimages that the rejection step actually accepts, and they modify the rejection-corrected Klein–GPV sampler to lower sampling cost. Security is stated as UF-CMA and SUF-CMA bounds in the classical random-oracle model.

Three things to hold. It is an unrefereed ePrint posting received on 26 September, and a tightened analysis of a scheme already selected for standardisation is exactly the sort of claim the community checks hard. The bounds are classical-ROM only; no quantum random-oracle statement is given. And the reduction is on the signature alone — Falcon's public keys are 897 and 1793 bytes and this does not change them.

glossary.definition: Drawing a random lattice point with probability falling off as a Gaussian in its distance from a target; it is how GPV-family signatures produce a short vector without revealing the secret basis.
The Gaussian width above which the distribution, reduced modulo the lattice, is close enough to uniform that a sample carries no information about which basis drew it.
The US federal standard that will specify Falcon. NIST still lists it as in development, unlike FIPS 203, 204 and 205, which were published on 13 August 2024.
Unforgeability under chosen-message attack: the attacker may obtain signatures on messages of its choosing and must still be unable to produce a valid signature on a new message.

items.title: Offload the matrix multiply and the matrix multiply becomes 1.6% of runtime
items.dek: Three researchers at the Technical University of Denmark bolted a 16×16 integer systolic array onto a RISC-V core, got 28 times the throughput on a dense neural-network layer, and then measured that the matrix multiply itself accounted for 1.64% of the cycles.
items.why_it_matters: The measurement says where accelerator engineering actually goes. With the array fast, about 80% of the cycles are the host core computing addresses, staging tiles between scratchpads and requantising results, so the next factor of two has to come from the plumbing and not from more multipliers. The compiler is the other wall: their hardware-semaphore allocation grows linearly with instruction count in the worst case, and that — rather than array size, memory or clock rate — is what stopped them running a larger network. Both are arguments for treating the data-orchestration path as the design.
items.background_md: A fixed-function matrix multiplier is easy to make fast and hard to keep fed. A systolic array consumes operands every cycle, so something has to generate addresses, stage tiles in local memory, and synchronise producer against consumer so neither reads a buffer the other is still writing. That bookkeeping is normally written by hand for each new accelerator, which is why each one arrives with a compiler of its own. Amdahl's law then sets the ceiling: the speedup available is bounded by the fraction of the work that was never moved onto the array.
items.deeper_md:
The prototype pairs a 16×16 int8 systolic array with a five-stage integer RISC-V core derived from riscv-Sodor over TileLink, on a Xilinx Kintex-7 xc7k160t at 104.602 MHz, with a 64 KB tier-0 scratchpad and 128 KB at each of tiers 1 and 2. The workload, taken from MLPerf-Tiny, sums 24 independent 16×16 int8 tiles in int32, adds bias, applies ReLU and requantises to int8. It runs in 127,348 cycles against 3,591,489 for the core alone — the 28× — of which the GEMM is 2,092 cycles, or 1.64%, and integer RISC-V work is 102,057 cycles, about 80%.

What to discount. The baseline is a single-issue in-order integer-only core, which is a soft thing to be 28× faster than; the workload is one synthetic layer; and the authors say the RISC-V lowering is unoptimised, which inflates the boot portion. They also report that larger workloads demanded an infeasible number of hardware semaphores, of which the prototype has 16. The direction is not new — the original TPU paper's own analysis concluded that tripling memory bandwidth would roughly triple achieved operations per second — but it is unusual to see the fraction printed.

glossary.definition: A grid of multiply-accumulate cells that pass operands to their neighbours each cycle, so one fetched operand is reused across a whole row or column instead of being read again for every multiply.
A counter in the hardware tracking how many buffers are full and how many are empty, letting a producer and a consumer hand data over without the processor polling for it.
Rescaling an int32 accumulator back down to int8 after a layer so the next layer's multipliers stay narrow; it is arithmetic the array does not do and the host core does.
A compiler infrastructure built around stacked, domain-specific intermediate representations called dialects, so a new accelerator can reuse the passes above it instead of getting a private compiler.

items.fab_angle: If MNF's custom IC ends up carrying a fixed-function block, this is the number to plan around: a 16×16 int8 array is within reach of a student design, and the cycles will go to whatever generates its addresses and moves its operands. The host-side plumbing is the project, not the accompaniment.

foundations.subtitle: Two bakes and a timer: the unglamorous steps around the exposure that decide how wide your line actually comes out.
foundations.tldr: The exposure tool gets the attention, but a printed linewidth is mostly decided by the three steps around it: the bake that drives solvent out of the resist, the optional bake after exposure that lets the latent image blur, and the develop step that turns chemistry into geometry. Each one is a temperature and a clock, and each one moves a dissolution rate that is steeply sensitive to both.

sections.heading: The film you expose is still part solvent
sections.body_md:
A freshly spun resist film is not the film you want to expose. MicroChemicals puts the residual solvent left after spin-coating at roughly 10% for a thin resist and up to 35% for a thick one; the softbake takes that down to a few per cent, typically 2–5%. That matters because solvent is a plasticiser. A wet film dissolves faster everywhere, including in the regions you never exposed, so contrast collapses; it also adheres worse and outgasses into whatever comes next.

The practical settings are narrower than you would guess. Hacker Fab's stepper flow bakes AZ-P4210 at 100 °C for 90 seconds on a hotplate after a 4000 rpm, 30-second coat. Caltech's teaching cleanroom uses 115 °C for one minute for a 1.6 µm S1813 coat, and 110 °C for 145 seconds for a 7 µm AZ 9260 coat. Underbake and you leave solvent behind. Overbake and you begin thermally decomposing the diazonaphthoquinone photoactive compound that makes the resist photosensitive in the first place. The window has a wall on each side, and the walls are about twenty degrees apart.

sections.heading: Solvent leaves from the top, so bakes do not simply scale
sections.body_md:
Solvent does not evaporate uniformly out of the bulk. It has to diffuse to the free surface, and as the top of the film dries, solvent diffusivity there drops sharply, so a solvent-depleted skin forms and the concentration gradient steepens underneath it. MicroChemicals describes exactly this depth profile, and it is the reason a bake is not a simple function of total heat delivered.

Fickian diffusion says the time to clear a film scales with the square of its thickness. Nothing in a real recipe table scales that way. Caltech's 7 µm AZ 9260 coat gets 145 seconds against 60 seconds for a 1.6 µm S1813 coat — 4.4 times the thickness for 2.4 times the bake. The gap is a deliberate compromise: you cannot push the temperature much higher without approaching decomposition, and you cannot bake all afternoon, so a thick-resist process accepts residual solvent deep in the film and compensates downstream. That is why thick-film recipes carry their own developer strengths. MicroChemicals recommends AZ 400K at 1:4 for AZ P4110, moving to 1:3.5 or 1:3 for thicker films.

sections.heading: The exposure leaves ridges, and the second bake sands them off
sections.body_md:
Light that reaches the substrate reflects. The reflected beam interferes with the incoming one, so the dose absorbed in the resist varies periodically through the film thickness, with intensity nodes spaced half a wavelength apart inside the resist. Two things follow. The developed sidewall comes out scalloped rather than straight, and the linewidth becomes a function of resist thickness — the swing curve every process engineer learns to hate.

A post-exposure bake fixes this by letting the latent image blur. Kirchauer's simulation treatment models it as ordinary Fickian diffusion of the photoactive compound, which amounts to convolving the post-exposure concentration profile with a Gaussian of diffusion length σ = √(2·D·t), and puts a conventional DQN post-exposure bake at around 100 °C for roughly ten minutes. The condition you want is a Goldilocks one that falls straight out of the convolution picture: σ must be at least comparable to half the standing-wave spacing, or the ridges survive, and it must stay well below the smallest feature you are printing, or the whole image washes out with them.

sections.heading: Chemically amplified resists use the same bake for the opposite reason
sections.body_md:
In a chemically amplified resist the exposure does not change solubility directly; it generates acid. The bake is where that acid catalytically deprotects the polymer, each acid molecule converting many sites before it is lost. So for these resists the post-exposure bake is not a smoothing step layered on top of the chemistry — it *is* the chemistry, and its temperature is a first-order process parameter.

Kirchauer's model carries two coupled species, reactive sites and acid, with a reaction order and rate constant, an acid-loss term, and a concentration-dependent acid diffusivity. For IBM's APEX-E resist at 90 °C the fitted values are a rate constant of 2.0 s⁻¹, a reaction order of 1.8, and a base acid diffusivity of 0.0933 nm²/s. Put sixty seconds into σ = √(2·D·t) and the acid travels about 3 nm. That is why a chemically amplified process holds plate temperature to a fraction of a degree, and why post-exposure delay is tracked: the model needs a surface-evaporation term because acid leaves the top of the film while you wait.

sections.heading: Development is an exponential dressed up as a timer
sections.body_md:
Developing is not a switch, it is a rate difference. In a diazonaphthoquinone–novolac resist the dissolution rate of exposed material can exceed that of unexposed material by a factor of 100 or more, and that ratio is the entire process window — it is what makes a resist a resist rather than a soluble film. Because it is a rate, the recipe has to pin both strength and temperature. Hacker Fab develops in AZ-400K diluted 3:1 with deionised water at 20 °C for 60 seconds, timing from the instant the chip enters the beaker, then quenches in deionised water for ten seconds.

Two chemistries are in common use and the difference is not cosmetic. AZ 400K is potassium-hydroxide based; AZ 2026 MIF is metal-ion-free tetramethylammonium hydroxide. The metal-ion-free family exists because sodium and potassium are mobile ions in a gate oxide, where they shift threshold voltage over the life of a device. And unexposed resist dissolves too, slowly — dark erosion — so over-developing does not merely clear more, it thins everything you meant to keep.

sections.heading: Adding up the error budget, and what a short flow leaves out
sections.body_md:
Line the contributions up and the track's role becomes obvious. Film thickness sets where you sit on the swing curve. Softbake sets the baseline dissolution rate. The post-exposure bake sets how far the latent image blurs. Develop time, developer strength and developer temperature set how far the dissolution front travels. Every one of those is a rate with a strong temperature dependence, which is why a production track is mostly a temperature-controlled machine with a robot in it.

The Hacker Fab flow is a short version of the same machine: HMDS prime at 4000 rpm for 20 seconds and 100 °C for 60 seconds, resist at 4000 rpm for 30 seconds, softbake 100 °C for 90 seconds, an 8-second exposure, a 60-second develop, then inspect at 5× or better. It has no post-exposure bake and no hard bake. Most g-, h- and i-line DNQ resists are not chemically amplified — MicroChemicals notes that among its AZ positive resists only AZ 40 XT and IPS 6050 are — so skipping the PEB is defensible, and what it costs is standing-wave sidewalls. Skipping the hard bake costs adhesion and etch resistance. Knowing which step you left out is how you know which defect you are looking at.

glossary.definition: The bake immediately after coating, typically 90–115 °C for 60–150 seconds, whose job is to drive residual casting solvent out of the resist film without decomposing the photoactive compound.

Casting solvent still trapped in the film. Roughly 10–35% right after spinning and 2–5% after a normal softbake; it plasticises the film and raises the dissolution rate of exposed and unexposed resist alike.

A bake between exposure and development. In a DNQ resist it diffuses the photoactive compound to wash out standing waves; in a chemically amplified resist it runs the acid-catalysed deprotection reaction that creates the solubility difference in the first place.

Periodic variation of absorbed dose through the resist thickness, caused by interference between the incoming light and the beam reflected off the substrate, with nodes half a wavelength apart in the resist. They print as scalloped sidewalls and make linewidth depend on film thickness.

The characteristic distance a diffusing species moves in time t with diffusivity D. It is the Gaussian width you convolve a latent image with to predict how much a bake blurs it — and it grows only as the square root of time, so doubling the blur costs four times the bake.
Dissolution of nominally unexposed resist during development. It sets a floor on usable develop time, because a long develop thins every feature you intended to keep, not only the ones you cleared.

An alkaline developer based on tetramethylammonium hydroxide rather than KOH or NaOH, used whenever the wafer will carry a MOS gate oxide, because sodium and potassium are mobile ions that drift under bias and shift threshold voltage.

foundations.try_this: Run the bake-plate sensitivity of your own flow. Coat three chips with AZ-P4210 at the SOP's 4000 rpm for 30 seconds, then softbake them at 90, 100 and 110 °C for the same 90 seconds. Expose all three identically, develop all three in 3:1 AZ-400K at 20 °C for 60 seconds, and measure the same test pattern's linewidth under a calibrated 5× or 10× objective. Plot linewidth against bake temperature: the slope is your hotplate's contribution to the CD budget, in nanometres per degree, and it tells you how tightly the plate has to be controlled before the stepper's own resolution is worth chasing.
